a: pray at all times and not grow weary
t: A parable with its point given first
p: Luke tells the reader the point before the story starts, which he rarely does.
b: Most parables leave their hearers to find the point. Here Luke states it in advance: keep praying and do not lose heart (the Greek enkakein means to give up, to go slack). The setting is the end of chapter 17, where Jesus has spoken of the days of the Son of Man coming suddenly. So the prayer in view is chiefly the cry of God's people for justice while they wait for him (18:7–8), not prayer for anything at all. Paul uses the same pairing of words: "pray without stopping" and "do not lose heart" (1 Thessalonians 5:17; 2 Corinthians 4:1, 16). Luke is the Gospel of prayer: Jesus prays at his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, at the transfiguration and on the cross (3:21; 6:12; 9:29; 23:46).

a: did not fear God and had no regard for people
t: A judge who answers to no one
p: Fearing God and respecting people was the standard description of a good judge. This one has neither.
b: The Law told judges to judge fairly because the judgment belongs to God (Deuteronomy 1:16–17), and King Jehoshaphat charged his judges, "So now let the dread of the LORD be on you" (2 Chronicles 19:7). A judge with no fear of God and no shame before people has no reason to do right. Josephus uses a very similar phrase for King Jehoiakim, who was "neither reverent toward God nor fair toward people" (Antiquities 10.83). In Jesus' day most local disputes were settled by Jewish courts or village elders, but money cases could also go before officials appointed by Herod's family or Rome. Kenneth Bailey notes that in Middle Eastern villages a widow without a male protector had little hope in such a court unless she could shame the judge into acting.

a: A widow
p: In the Law, the widow is the classic person with no one to protect her, and God's special concern.
b: Again and again the Law and the Prophets name the widow, the orphan and the foreigner as the people God himself defends: "Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly" (Exodus 22:22; compare Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 1:17, 23). A widow had no husband to speak for her in court, and often no money for a bribe. Luke shows special care for widows: Anna (2:36–38), the widow of Zarephath (4:25–26), the widow of Nain (7:11–17), the widow whose house the scribes devour and the widow who gives her last coins (20:47; 21:1–4), and the widows of the church in Acts 6:1 and 9:39–41. In this parable the weakest person in town is the one who will not give up.

a: Defend my rights
p: The KJV's "avenge me" sounds like revenge. The word is a legal one: give me the justice I am owed.
b: The verb ekdikeō and its noun ekdikēsis run through the parable four times (18:3, 5, 7, 8). The KJV says "avenge me of mine adversary," which suggests personal revenge. In legal Greek the word means to settle a case in someone's favor, to see that a person gets their rights. The antidikos is the opposing party in a lawsuit (compare 12:58; Matthew 5:25). The same family of words returns in 21:22, where Jerusalem's fall is called "days of retribution": the justice God does is not only rescue for his people but judgment on wrong.

a: give me a black eye
t: A black eye, or just worn out?
p: The verb is a boxing word: to hit under the eye. Many translations soften it to "wear me out."
b: Hypōpiazō means to strike someone in the face, to give a black eye; Paul uses it of a boxer beating his own body into shape (1 Corinthians 9:27). Here it can be literal (the judge fears she will finally come and hit him) or figurative (she will "beat him down," or shame him, give him a black eye in public). The phrase eis telos can mean "in the end" or "continually," so the clause can also be read "by coming again and again she will wear me out." The Plain keeps the boxing image because it is comic: a judge who fears no one is afraid of a widow. Either way, he acts for his own comfort, not for justice.

a: the Lord said
p: Luke often calls Jesus "the Lord" in his own narration, something Mark and Matthew almost never do.
b: In Mark and Matthew the narrator calls Jesus "Jesus." Luke, writing for readers who already confess him as Lord, often uses ho kyrios in the story itself (7:13, 19; 10:1, 39, 41; 11:39; 12:42; 13:15; 17:5–6; 19:8; 22:61). Here "the Lord" stands right beside the parable's crooked judge and the God who judges rightly: the one telling the story is himself the Son of Man who will come (18:8).

a: the crooked judge
t: From the lesser to the greater
p: The parable argues: if even a bad judge gives in, how much more will God, who is just and loves his people.
b: This is the Jewish argument the rabbis called qal wa-chomer, "light and heavy": what is true in the lesser case is true all the more in the greater. Jesus uses it in 11:13 ("if you, evil as you are..."). God is not like the judge; he is the opposite. The point is not that pestering God wears him down, but that God's people can be sure he will act. Some readers take the widow as a model of persistence; others, such as Kenneth Bailey, stress the contrast between the judge and God. A minority reading (Herzog) makes the widow the hero who shames a corrupt system into justice, with no figure for God at all.

a: his chosen, who call out to him day and night
p: Behind the parable stands Sirach 35, where God hears the widow and will not hold back from the wicked.
b: In Sirach 35 (verses 17–22 in the NRSV numbering used here; other Bibles number them differently), the Lord does not ignore the widow's complaint, the prayer of the humble pierces the clouds, and the Lord "will not delay" or be patient with the oppressors, using the same verb Luke uses here (makrothymeō). Sirach is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians and stands in the Apocrypha for Protestants. The cry "day and night" is the cry of the martyrs under the altar in Revelation 6:10, "How long?" and of Anna in the temple (2:37). "His chosen" is the word Mark and Matthew use in the end-time discourse for God's people (Mark 13:20, 27).

a: Is he slow to act for them?
t: Patient with them, or slow to help?
p: The last clause of 18:7 can be read three ways; translations differ.
b: Kai makrothymei ep' autois literally says "and is he patient over them?" It can mean (1) "will he delay over them?", expecting the answer no, which fits 18:8 "without delay"; (2) "even though he is patient with them," that is, God bears long with his people; or (3) "is he patient toward the oppressors?", as in Sirach 35:22 (NRSV numbering), where God will not be patient with the wicked. The Plain takes the first reading, which most modern translations follow, but the tension is real: God answers "without delay," yet the church has waited a long time (2 Peter 3:8–9, where makrothymeō is the Lord's patience, giving time to repent).

a: will he find faith on the earth at all?
t: The question that turns the parable around
p: After promising that God will act, Jesus asks whether his own people will still be trusting when he comes.
b: The Greek has "the faith": the kind of persistent, praying trust the widow showed. The particle ara expects a doubtful answer. The parable began as an encouragement to pray and ends as a warning: the question is not whether God is faithful, but whether the waiting church will be. Matthew's discourse has the same worry: "the love of many will go cold" (Matthew 24:12). Some read the verse as pessimism about the end (widespread unbelief before Christ returns, as in 2 Thessalonians 2:3); others read it as a call to the hearer, "will he find it in you?"

a: felt sure in themselves that they were righteous
t: Not a parable against all Pharisees
p: Luke names the target: anyone who trusts in his own righteousness and despises others.
b: Luke's introduction does not say the hearers were Pharisees; it describes an attitude that a Pharisee in the story happens to show. Many Christian readings have turned the Pharisee into a picture of Judaism and the tax collector into the Christian, which Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine have shown to be a caricature: most Jews of the time did not think they earned God's favor by fasting. Jesus had already warned the Pharisees, "You justify yourselves in people's eyes, but God knows your hearts" (16:15); compare Paul's "not having a righteousness of my own" (Philippians 3:9).

a: a Pharisee
t: Two men at the hour of prayer
p: The two men likely came at one of the daily sacrifices, when people gathered in the temple courts to pray.
b: Public prayer in the temple centered on the morning and afternoon burnt offerings, the tamid (Exodus 29:38–42), when incense was offered and the people prayed outside (1:10; Acts 3:1, "the hour of prayer, the ninth hour"). Bailey suggests that both men came to the atonement sacrifice, which explains the tax collector's plea in 18:13. The Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to keeping the Law carefully in daily life, admired by many ordinary Jews (Josephus, Antiquities 18.15). Tax collectors were Jews who collected tolls and taxes for Herod Antipas or Rome, often by overcharging, and were treated as collaborators and cheats.

a: took his stand and prayed these words to himself
t: Prayed to himself, or stood by himself?
p: The phrase "to himself" can go with "prayed" or with "stood"; the manuscripts even place it differently.
b: The Greek statheis pros heauton tauta prosēucheto can mean "standing, he prayed these things to himself" (silently, or with himself as his real audience) or "standing by himself, he prayed these things," that is, apart from others so as not to be made unclean by them. The words are ordered differently in different manuscripts, and some leave "to himself" out, a sign that copyists also found it awkward. Either way Luke's irony is the same: a prayer addressed to God that is mostly about the man praying.

a: 'God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humanity
p: Thanking God for one's lot in life was a real form of Jewish prayer. The problem here is the contempt.
b: The Talmud preserves a prayer of Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah on leaving the house of study: "I give thanks before you, LORD my God, that you have set my portion with those who sit in the house of study and not with those who sit on street corners" (Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 28b). The Dead Sea Scrolls' Thanksgiving Hymns thank God for setting the speaker apart. Such prayers thank God, not oneself, for a life of study. The Pharisee in the parable begins the same way but turns it into a list of other people's sins and his own merits, and ends by despising the man behind him. Jesus aims the story at that turn, not at gratitude.

a: Twice a week I fast
t: Fasting and tithing beyond the Law
p: The Law required one fast a year and tithes on crops. This man goes far beyond both.
b: The Law of Moses commands only one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31). Devout Jews also fasted on other days, and the Didache, an early Christian manual, tells believers not to fast "with the hypocrites" on Mondays and Thursdays but on Wednesdays and Fridays (Didache 8:1), which shows that twice-weekly fasting on those days was a known Jewish practice. The tithe was owed on grain, wine, oil and herds (Deuteronomy 14:22–23); the Pharisees tithed even herbs (11:42) and anything bought whose tithe was in doubt. Everything the man says is true and good. The parable never questions his deeds, only his trust in them.

a: kept striking his chest
p: Striking one's chest was a gesture of grief and repentance, usually made by women at funerals.
b: In the ancient Near East beating the breast was a sign of mourning (23:48, the crowd at the cross). Bailey notes that in Middle Eastern culture it is mostly women who beat their chests; for a man to do it shows extreme anguish. The tax collector does not come near the sanctuary, does not lift his eyes (compare Ezra 9:6, "I am ashamed and humiliated to lift my face toward you"), and names himself not "a" sinner but "the" sinner, as if he were the only one.

a: be gracious to me, the sinner
p: The verb is not the usual "have mercy." It is the word for atonement: may God's anger be turned aside.
b: The tax collector does not say eleēson, "have mercy," as the blind man does (18:38). He says hilasthēti, from hilaskomai, the verb of atonement: to make or be favorable through a sacrifice that covers sin. The Septuagint uses it for God forgiving his people (Psalm 79:9 LXX, "be gracious to our sins"), and Hebrews 2:17 uses it of Christ making atonement. The related noun is the "atonement lid" of the ark (Hebrews 9:5). If the scene takes place at the hour of the daily sacrifice, the man is asking that the atonement being made at the altar would cover him. The older English "be merciful" is right, but hides this link.
r: Psalm 79:9; Psalm 51:1; Hebrews 2:17; Hebrews 9:5; Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2

a: who went down to his home justified
p: "Justified" is Paul's great word, and Luke uses it here in the same sense: declared right with God.
b: Dedikaiōmenos means "declared righteous, put in the right." The man who trusted in his righteousness (18:9) goes home without it; the man who asked only for atonement goes home with it. Many scholars see here the closest the Gospels come to Paul's teaching that God "justifies the ungodly" (Romans 4:5). Others note that "justify" was already an Old Testament word for God's verdict (Isaiah 50:8; Psalm 143:2) and that Jesus' point fits Jewish teaching on repentance. The Greek par' ekeinon, literally "beside that one," is read by most scholars as "rather than the other," not "more than": only one went home right with God, and the Plain follows that. Amy-Jill Levine argues for another possibility: para with the accusative can also mean "alongside" or even "because of," so the tax collector might be justified alongside the Pharisee, or thanks to him, in line with the Jewish idea that the merit of the righteous benefits the whole community. Few scholars follow her, but the grammar allows it (see the J view on this chapter). On what justification means in the church debate, see the card at Genesis 15:6; the card on this chapter asks only what this scene adds.

a: Everyone who raises himself up will be brought low
p: Jesus has said this before, at a dinner (14:11). It is the theme of Mary's song.
b: The same saying closes the parable of the places at the wedding feast (14:11) and appears in Matthew's warning against the scribes (Matthew 23:12, in nearly the same words). It sums up a reversal that runs through all of Luke: "He has pulled rulers down from thrones and raised the lowly high" (1:52), blessings for the poor and woes for the rich (6:20–26), Lazarus and the rich man (16:25). The passive verbs ("will be brought low ... will be raised up") leave the action to God. The idea is rooted in the Old Testament: Proverbs 29:23; Ezekiel 21:26; 1 Samuel 2:7–8.

a: even their babies
p: Luke changes Mark's "little children" to "babies," infants in arms. This is one reason the verse is cited in the infant baptism debate.
b: Mark and Matthew have paidia, "little children." Luke writes ta brephē, the word for a newborn or a baby (2:12, 16; Acts 7:19), and adds "even": people brought even their infants. Then in 18:16 he returns to Mark's paidia. Luke also drops Mark's note that Jesus grew angry and took the children in his arms (Mark 10:14, 16). Because Luke's word is "babies," the passage has been used in the debate over baptizing infants since the early church. That debate is set out on the card at Matthew 19:14.

a: the way a child does
t: Receiving the kingdom like a child
p: What it means to receive the kingdom "as a child" has been read in several ways.
b: Readers have taken it to mean receiving the kingdom with a child's trust, with a child's humility, or with a child's helplessness: a child brings nothing and simply receives. In the ancient world children were not idealized; they had no status. Coming right after the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, Luke's placement points to the last reading: the kingdom is received as a gift by those who have nothing to show for themselves (18:13–14). This is where Luke rejoins Mark's order after his long journey section (9:51–18:14).

a: A leader
p: Only Luke calls him a leader (archōn); only Matthew calls him young. The traditional "rich young ruler" combines all three Gospels.
b: Archōn can mean a member of a ruling council, a synagogue official (8:41) or a leading Pharisee (14:1). Mark says only "a man," Matthew "a young man" (Matthew 19:20), and Luke "a leader." The familiar name "the rich young ruler" combines all three. Luke's detail sets him among the leaders who will reject Jesus (23:13, 35; 24:20), yet Jesus treats him with respect. His question is the same one the lawyer asked in 10:25, except that this man adds "good," but the answer goes a different way.

a: Why do you call me good?
t: Is Jesus denying that he is good?
p: Luke keeps Mark's wording, which Matthew changed. Readers have long asked what it implies.
b: Luke follows Mark word for word (Mark 10:18), while Matthew reworded it to "Why are you asking me about the good?" (Matthew 19:17). The early church read the saying in several ways: Jesus is testing whether the man sees that he is speaking to God; or Jesus speaks as a human being who gives all glory to the Father; or he simply refuses flattery, since in Jewish usage "good" was a title for God. Arians in the 300s used the verse to argue the Son was less than the Father; their opponents answered with the first reading. The Mark 10:18 note gives more detail.

a: 'You must not commit adultery. You must not murder.
p: Luke lists adultery before murder, an order found in some Greek manuscripts of Deuteronomy, in Paul and in James.
b: The Hebrew of Exodus 20:13–14 and Deuteronomy 5:17–18 puts "murder" first. Some Septuagint manuscripts of Deuteronomy 5 put adultery first, and so do Romans 13:9, James 2:11 and Philo. Luke may follow that Greek order. Like Mark and Matthew, he lists only commandments about other people, and leaves out coveting, the one commandment that money breaks from the inside. Mark's extra "You must not cheat" (Mark 10:19) is not in Luke.

a: Sell everything you have and share it out among the poor
p: Luke sharpens Mark's "whatever you have" to "everything." Is this for every disciple?
b: Luke adds "everything" (panta) and uses diadidōmi, "distribute, share out," the word for the church's sharing in Acts 4:35. Earlier in Luke, Jesus told all would-be disciples to "say goodbye to all his possessions" (14:33) and to "sell your property and give alms" (12:33). Yet Zacchaeus gives half (19:8) and Jesus calls that salvation. So readers ask whether the command is for this man, for those called to a special life, or for all. Matthew 19:21 frames it as "if you wish to be perfect"; the churches' different answers are set out on the card there.

a: He was a very rich man
p: In Mark and Matthew the man goes away grieving. In Luke he stays, sad, and hears the rest.
b: Luke leaves out "he went away" (Mark 10:22; Matthew 19:22). The leader is still there when Jesus speaks of camels and needles, so the hard words are spoken to his face, and the story stays open: the reader does not learn what he decided. Luke follows it at once with a rich man who does respond, Zacchaeus (19:1–10).

a: a needle's eye
t: Luke's needle and the medical argument
p: Luke uses belonē, a word for a needle that was also used of a surgeon's needle. That was once taken as proof that a doctor wrote Luke.
b: Mark and Matthew have rhaphis, a sewing needle; Luke has belonē (and trēma, "hole"). In 1882 W. K. Hobart argued that this and hundreds of other words showed that Luke wrote as a physician, "Luke the dear doctor" (Colossians 4:14). Henry Cadbury answered in 1919–1920 that almost all these words also appear in Greek writers who were not doctors, such as Josephus and Plutarch. Most scholars accept Cadbury's verdict: Luke's vocabulary is that of an educated Greek writer, and it neither proves nor disproves the tradition. On the camel and the needle themselves, see Mark 10:25.

a: What is impossible from the human side is possible with God
p: The angel told Mary the same thing (1:37). Luke frames his Gospel with it.
b: Gabriel's word to Mary, "no word that comes from God will be powerless" (1:37), uses the same Greek root as "impossible" here, and echoes God's word to Abraham about Sarah: "Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?" (Genesis 18:14). Here the same truth answers the question of salvation for the rich. In Luke the impossible happens at once, in the next story: a rich chief tax collector is saved (19:9).

a: wife
p: Only Luke lists a wife among the things disciples may leave. Peter, for one, was married.
b: Mark's list has homes, brothers, sisters, mother, father, children and farms (Mark 10:29). Luke drops sisters and farms, sums up the parents in one word, and adds "wife," as he does in 14:26 ("his wife"). Peter was married (4:38; 1 Corinthians 9:5), and Paul says the apostles took their wives with them on their travels. So "leaving" probably meant long absences on mission, not divorce. The verse has been read in support of clerical celibacy and religious vows; see the cards on celibacy at Matthew 8:14 and 19:12.

a: eternal life in the age that is coming
p: Jesus speaks the common Jewish language of "this age" and "the age to come."
b: Jewish teachers divided time into "this age" (ha'olam hazeh) and "the age to come" (ha'olam haba), the new world after God's judgment (compare 4 Ezra 7:50, "the Most High has made not one age but two"). "Eternal life" is literally "the life of the age," the life that belongs to the age to come. Jesus promises disciples both: a new family in this present time (the church; Acts 2:44–47) and that life in the next. Luke does not have Mark's "along with persecutions," though he will tell of plenty in Acts.

a: everything the prophets wrote about the Son of Man will be carried out
p: Only Luke says the suffering fulfills the prophets. This becomes the risen Jesus' teaching at Emmaus.
b: Mark's and Matthew's third prediction says nothing about Scripture. Luke adds that everything written "through the prophets" will be completed (telesthēsetai, the same root as Jesus' last word in John 19:30). After the resurrection Jesus will explain this to the two at Emmaus and to the eleven: "Did the Messiah not have to suffer these things?" (24:25–27, 44–46). Luke does not say which prophets; the early church read Isaiah 53, Psalm 22 and Psalm 118:22 this way (Acts 8:32–35; 4:11). The Greek dative "to the Son of Man" can mean "about" him or "for" him.

a: He will be handed over to the Gentiles
p: Luke's third prediction names only the Gentiles, not the chief priests and scribes as in Mark.
b: In Mark and Matthew the Son of Man is handed over first to the chief priests and scribes, who condemn him and hand him to the Gentiles. Luke mentions only the Gentiles, the Romans who will mock, beat and crucify him. Luke's earlier predictions name the elders, chief priests and scribes (9:22), and his passion story does show the temple leaders handing Jesus to Pilate (23:1). So the shorter wording is not an attempt to clear them, but it does keep the focus on what Rome would do. Luke alone adds "insult him" (hybristhēsetai).

a: they took in none of it
p: Luke says three times that the disciples did not understand. The passive "was hidden" may mean God kept it from them for now.
b: Luke repeats the point in three ways, as he did after the second prediction (9:45). "Was kept hidden" is a passive that many readers take as God's doing: the meaning of the cross could not be grasped until after the resurrection, when the risen Jesus "opened their minds" (24:45). Others read it as the disciples' own blindness, which the next story, a blind man who sees and follows, is placed to contrast. Both can be true: Luke likes stories in which sight is given (24:31).

a: When he was getting close to Jericho
p: Luke places the healing as Jesus approaches Jericho; Mark and Matthew, as he leaves it. One man or two?
b: Mark has one blind man, Bartimaeus, as Jesus leaves Jericho (Mark 10:46); Matthew has two men as he leaves (Matthew 20:29–30); Luke has one unnamed man as Jesus approaches. Luke probably moved the healing earlier so that the Zacchaeus story, in the town itself, could follow. Some harmonizers have suggested that there were two Jerichos, the old town on the tell and Herod's new town with its palaces about two kilometers south, so Jesus could leave one and enter the other. Others suggested two healings. Most modern scholars see a writer's arrangement and do not try to harmonize.

a: Jesus, Son of David, show me mercy!
p: The blind man uses a royal title for the Messiah, just before Jesus is hailed as King (19:38).
b: "Son of David" meant the promised king from David's line (2 Samuel 7:12–16). The Psalms of Solomon, written about 50 BC, pray that the Lord will raise up for Israel their king, the son of David (Psalms of Solomon 17:21). In Luke the angel promised Mary that God would give her son "the throne of David his father" (1:32). Later Jewish tradition also linked Solomon, David's son, with healing and power over demons. The blind man's title prepares for the royal entry to Jerusalem (19:38) and for Jesus' question about David's son (20:41–44).
r: 1:32; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1; 19:38; 20:41–44; Psalms of Solomon 17:21; Mark 10:47

a: The people walking in front
p: In Luke the ones who try to silence the man are those walking in front, the leaders of the procession.
b: Mark says "many" told him to hush; Luke specifies "the people walking in front," perhaps the disciples or pilgrims leading the way. Luke tells a series of stories in which people with no standing are almost shut out: the babies the disciples scold (18:15), the blind man the leaders silence, and Zacchaeus blocked by the crowd (19:3). In each, Jesus stops and welcomes the one pushed aside.

a: Your faith has saved you
p: The same Greek word means both "heal" and "save." Luke uses this exact sentence four times.
b: Hē pistis sou sesōken se, "your faith has saved you," is said to the woman who anointed Jesus' feet (7:50), the woman with the flow of blood (8:48), the Samaritan healed of skin disease (17:19) and this blind man. In three of these the saving is a healing, and in 7:50 it is forgiveness. Luke keeps the word open so the reader sees that bodily healing and salvation belong together. The Zacchaeus story ends with the same verb: the Son of Man came "to look for what was lost and to save it" (19:10).

a: giving glory to God
p: Luke regularly ends a miracle with the healed person and the crowd praising God.
b: Praise is Luke's refrain: the shepherds (2:20), the paralyzed man and the crowd (5:25–26), the widow's townspeople at Nain (7:16), the bent woman (13:13), the Samaritan (17:15), and here both the man and "all the people" (pas ho laos, Luke's word for Israel as God's people). The Gospel ends with the disciples in the temple "praising God" (24:53). The healed man "began following" Jesus, on the road up to Jerusalem.

a: He went into Jericho
p: Herod's Jericho was a rich oasis town of palms and balsam, with royal palaces and a customs post on the road.
b: Jericho lies about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Jerusalem and nearly a kilometer lower. Herod the Great built winter palaces there, and his son Archelaus rebuilt them (Josephus, Antiquities 17.340). The oasis was famous for its date palms and its balsam, an expensive perfume and medicine (Josephus, War 4.459–475). It sat on the main road for pilgrims from Galilee and Perea who crossed the Jordan to avoid Samaria, which made it a natural place to collect tolls and taxes on goods. The road from there climbs steeply to Jerusalem (10:30).

a: He was the head of the tax collectors
p: Architelōnēs appears nowhere else in Greek literature that has survived. Zacchaeus probably ran a district's tax contract.
b: Under the Romans and Herod's sons, the right to collect tolls and certain taxes was sold to contractors, who hired local agents and kept what they collected above the price of the contract. A "chief tax collector" likely held such a contract and employed others, which explains his wealth. His Hebrew name, Zakkai, means "pure, innocent" (Ezra 2:9 has a family of that name), an irony Luke's readers who knew Hebrew might enjoy. Levi, the tax collector who followed Jesus earlier (5:27–32), was probably one of the lower agents.

a: he was a short man
p: The Greek could mean Jesus was short, but most readers take it of Zacchaeus, who then climbs a tree.
b: The Greek says only "because in stature he was small." Grammatically the "he" could be Jesus, and a few writers have suggested that. But the next verse, where Zacchaeus climbs a tree to see over the crowd, makes most sense if he was the short one. Hēlikia can also mean age or maturity: at 2:52 the Plain renders it "maturity" ("Jesus kept moving forward in wisdom and in maturity"), though others take it there as stature. Here "short" fits. Climbing a tree was undignified for a wealthy man, but Zacchaeus does not care.

a: fig-mulberry tree
p: Not the North American sycamore. The sykomorea is a wide, low fig tree with spreading branches.
b: The sykomorea is Ficus sycomorus, the sycamore fig, a large evergreen of the warm Jordan valley and the coast, with a short trunk and low, wide branches that are easy to climb. Its small figs were food for the poor; the prophet Amos was a "dresser of sycamore figs" (Amos 7:14), and King David had overseers for them (1 Chronicles 27:28). It is not the plane tree or the maple called "sycamore" in Britain and America. Visitors to Jericho today are shown an old sycamore fig said to be Zacchaeus' tree.

a: Today I have to stay in your house
p: Two of Luke's key words meet here: "today," the day salvation arrives, and "must," God's plan.
b: "Today" (sēmeron) marks the moments when salvation arrives in Luke: "today ... a Savior was born for you" (2:11), "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled" (4:21), "Today salvation has come to this household" (19:9), "today you will be with me in paradise" (23:43). "I have to" (dei) is Luke's word for what God's plan requires: the Son of Man "must" suffer (9:22; 17:25; 24:7, 26). Jesus invites himself as a guest, as if staying with this man were part of God's plan.

a: they all started grumbling
p: The same complaint was made at Levi's feast and before the parables of the lost (5:30; 15:2).
b: The Pharisees and scribes grumbled when Jesus ate with tax collectors at Levi's house (5:30), and again when he welcomed sinners (15:2). Here "all" grumble, including, presumably, his own followers. Luke uses the same verb family the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel's grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8; Numbers 14:27). To stay in a man's house was to share his table and his honor. Jesus' answer, "to look for what was lost and to save it" (19:10), sums up the three parables told after the grumbling in chapter 15.

a: half of what I own I give to the poor
p: Zacchaeus speaks in the present tense: "I give ... I pay back." Is he promising to change, or defending what he already does?
b: Most readers take the present tenses as a resolve made on the spot: "Here and now I give half." Zacchaeus repents, gives generously, and repays far beyond what the Law asks. Others, including Joseph Fitzmyer and Joel Green, read them as describing his habit: Zacchaeus defends himself against the crowd's charge that he is a sinner, and Jesus vindicates him as a true son of Abraham. On that reading the story is about Jesus overturning a label, not about a conversion. The Greek allows both. Either way, the man Jesus says salvation has reached is a man whose money is going to the poor.

a: by false charges
p: Sykophanteō means to squeeze money out of people by false charges or threats, a known tax collectors' trick.
b: The verb is the one John the Baptist used when he told soldiers, "Don't squeeze money out of anyone by force or by false charges" (3:14). A tax collector could overvalue goods, threaten an informer's charge, or demand bribes. "If I have" is a Greek conditional that treats the case as real, "whatever I have taken." Fourfold repayment goes beyond the Law: Leviticus 6:5 and Numbers 5:7 require the full amount plus a fifth. Fourfold is the penalty for a stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1), which David himself named for the rich man in Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12:6).

a: he too is a son of Abraham
p: Jesus restores a despised Jew to his place in Israel, as he did the bent woman, "a daughter of Abraham" (13:16).
b: Tax collectors were treated by many fellow Jews as having cut themselves off from the people. Jesus' words put Zacchaeus back among the children of Abraham, the heirs of God's promise. Luke uses the same phrase for the woman healed on the Sabbath, "a daughter of Abraham" (13:16). Jesus gives a reason ("for," kathoti): salvation has come because Zacchaeus belongs to Abraham's family, and Jesus came to seek the lost of that family (19:10). John the Baptist warned that descent from Abraham alone saves no one (3:8), and the rich man in Hades called Abraham "father" in vain (16:24). Zacchaeus shows the kind of son Abraham has: one who repents and shares. Salvation comes "to this household," the family and servants as well, as with the households of Cornelius, Lydia and the jailer in Acts.

a: to look for what was lost and to save it
t: The shepherd who seeks the lost
p: Jesus takes up God's words in Ezekiel 34: God himself will seek the lost sheep that Israel's shepherds neglected.
b: In Ezekiel 34 God condemns Israel's leaders as bad shepherds and promises, "I will look for the lost" (Ezekiel 34:16, the same Greek words in the Septuagint: to apolōlos zētēsō), and to set over them one shepherd, "my servant David" (Ezekiel 34:23). The neuter "what was lost" covers every kind of lost thing, as in the parables of the sheep, the coin and the son (15:4–32). This verse is often called the summary of the whole Gospel of Luke. Matthew 18:11 has a similar saying only in later manuscripts.

a: they supposed the kingdom of God was about to show itself at any moment
p: Luke says the parable corrects an expectation: that the kingdom would appear as soon as Jesus reached Jerusalem.
b: Pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for Passover, the festival of freedom, with a man some called Son of David (18:38), could easily expect him to take the throne there. Luke says the parable was told to correct this. Many scholars see Luke's own concern for his readers, who lived after Jesus' death and resurrection and were still waiting for his return: the king must first go away and receive his kingdom, and his servants must be faithful in the meantime. The disciples ask the same question after the resurrection: "Lord, is this the time you are giving the kingdom back to Israel?" (Acts 1:6).

a: to have the kingship given to him and then come back
t: A real prince who went to Rome
p: Jesus' hearers knew this story: Archelaus, Herod's son, went to Rome in 4 BC to be made king, and the Jews sent envoys to oppose him.
b: When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus had to sail to Rome to have his father's will confirmed by Augustus. A delegation of fifty Jews followed him to ask the emperor not to make him king (Josephus, Antiquities 17.299–314; War 2.80–92). Augustus gave him Judea with the lesser title of ethnarch, and on his return he punished his opponents. Before he left, Archelaus had put down a riot at Passover by killing about three thousand people in the temple courts (War 2.10–13). Archelaus had rebuilt the royal palace at Jericho, where Jesus told this parable. Herod Antipas had also gone to Rome to seek the crown. For Jesus' hearers the parable's nobleman was a familiar, and feared, figure.

a: ten minas
p: A mina was a hundred drachmas, about a hundred days' wages. Each slave got one, a modest sum compared with Matthew's talents.
b: The Greek mina (mna) was worth 100 drachmas; a drachma, like the Roman denarius, was about a laborer's daily wage (Matthew 20:2). So a mina was roughly four months' wages. In Matthew's parable of the talents, the master gives five, two and one talents, and a talent was sixty minas (Matthew 25:15). Luke's master gives each of ten slaves the same small amount, "a very little" (19:17), to test faithfulness. The verb pragmateuomai means to do business, to trade: the money is to be put to work.

a: We do not want this man to rule as king over us
p: Luke's parable weaves a story about a rejected king into a story about faithful and unfaithful slaves.
b: Remove 19:12b, 14–15a and 27, and what is left is close to Matthew's parable of the talents. Many scholars think Luke (or the tradition before him) has combined two parables: one about money entrusted to slaves, and one about a nobleman whose citizens reject him. Others think Jesus told one parable that used the Archelaus story. In Luke's setting the two strands fit: Jesus is about to be rejected as king by Jerusalem's leaders (19:39, 47; 23:2–3, 37–38), and his followers must be faithful while he is away. Matthew's version and its setting are compared on Luke's settings card for this parable.

a: you will have authority over ten towns
p: The faithful slaves are rewarded with more to look after, not with leisure.
b: In Matthew the reward is to "come in to your master's joy" (Matthew 25:21); in Luke it is rule over towns, as a new king might hand out governorships to loyal servants. The reward matches the faithfulness: ten minas, ten towns; five minas, five towns. Jesus will promise the Twelve, "you will sit on thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel" (22:30), and Revelation pictures the faithful reigning with Christ (Revelation 2:26; 22:5). The principle is the one stated in 16:10: "Someone who is faithful in the smallest things is faithful in big things as well."

a: wrapped in a cloth
p: Jewish law later held that money wrapped in a cloth was carelessly kept; burying it was the safe way.
b: The soudarion was a cloth for wiping sweat, a handkerchief or neck cloth (Acts 19:12; John 11:44; 20:7). In Matthew the third slave buries the talent (Matthew 25:25). Joachim Jeremias pointed out that rabbinic law later counted burying as the safest way to keep money in trust, so that a keeper who buried it was not liable if it was stolen, while one who tied it up in a cloth was (Mishnah Bava Metzia 3:10; Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 42a). If that rule was known in Jesus' day, Luke's slave was not even careful: he kept the mina in the least safe way.

a: You are an exacting man
p: Austēros means severe, strict, demanding, someone who takes all he can.
b: English "austere" comes from this word, but in Greek it describes a man who is hard and grasping, the kind who collects what he never deposited. The slave's accusation describes the nobleman as the hearers knew such rulers to be. The master does not deny it (19:22); he judges the slave by his own words. Readers have long asked whether the master is meant to picture God at all. See the note on 19:27.

a: on the bankers' table
p: Money changers and bankers sat at tables (trapezai); putting money "on the table" meant depositing it to earn interest.
b: Greek trapeza, "table," is still the Greek word for a bank. Bankers in the ancient world took deposits and lent at interest. The Law forbade Israelites to charge interest to fellow Israelites (Deuteronomy 23:19–20), but by the first century loans at interest were common, and Hillel's prosbul allowed debts to survive the seventh-year release. The master's point: even the least effort would have brought some return.

a: he has ten minas!
p: The bystanders object that the first slave already has plenty. Some manuscripts leave this verse out.
b: The protest makes the listener feel the strangeness of the master's justice before he states his rule (19:26). Because the verse interrupts the speech, some early witnesses lack it (see the variant). If it is original, it is one of several places where Luke lets a listener inside the story voice what the reader is thinking (compare 15:29–30).

a: everyone who has something will be given more
p: Jesus said this earlier about hearing the word (8:18). Here it is about using what one is given.
b: The saying appears in five places in the Gospels (Mark 4:25; Matthew 13:12; Matthew 25:29; 8:18; here). In 8:18 it is about how one listens: whoever takes in the word receives more understanding. Here it is about faithfulness: whoever uses what the king entrusted will be trusted with more. It is not a rule of economics, "the rich get richer," but a rule of the kingdom about gifts received from God.

a: bring them here and slaughter them in front of me
p: The parable ends with a massacre. Readers disagree on whether the cruel king stands for Jesus.
b: The verb katasphazō means to slaughter or butcher, a word for sacrificial animals and massacres. The traditional reading takes the nobleman as Christ, who goes to heaven to receive his kingdom and will return to judge, and the slaughtered enemies as those who reject him; many have added Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70 (19:41–44). Others note that Jesus never portrays God by an unjust figure without saying so (18:6), and that the parable's details fit Archelaus, who did kill his opponents. Readers such as William Herzog and Luise Schottroff read the parable as a warning about how earthly kings behave, with the third slave as the one who refuses to join the system. A middle view (Snodgrass and many others) holds that the nobleman is Christ, but that the imagery of a king's vengeance is borrowed, not a picture of Christ's character. No church teaches that the verse permits killing unbelievers.

a: climbing the road up to Jerusalem
p: The road from Jericho to Jerusalem rises about a kilometer in 25 kilometers, through desert hills.
b: Jericho is about 250 meters below sea level and Jerusalem about 750 meters above it. The ancient road climbed through the Judean wilderness, the setting of the good Samaritan (10:30). Luke's long journey to Jerusalem, which began in 9:51 when Jesus "set his face" toward the city, ends here. Jesus "walked on in front" (emprosthen), leading the way, as he did in Mark 10:32.

a: Bethphage and Bethany
p: Two villages on the eastern slopes of the Mount of Olives, the last stop before Jerusalem on the road from Jericho.
b: Bethany lies about three kilometers (two miles) from Jerusalem (John 11:18), the home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus in John. Bethphage, "house of unripe figs," was nearer the summit; the rabbis treated it as the outer limit of Jerusalem for certain purposes. Luke places the ascension "as far as Bethany" (24:50), so the Gospel's last scene happens where the entry into Jerusalem begins.

a: one that no person has ever yet sat on
p: Animals set apart for sacred use had to be ones never put to work.
b: The red heifer had to be one "on which a yoke has never come" (Numbers 19:2; compare Deuteronomy 21:3), and the Philistines returned the ark on a cart drawn by cows never yoked (1 Samuel 6:7). An unridden colt fits a sacred, royal use. The rabbis also said no one else may ride a king's horse. Luke, unlike Matthew (21:4–5) and John (12:14–15), does not quote Zechariah 9:9, but the colt brings it to mind.

a: its owners
p: Luke makes a word play: the colt's "lords" (owners) ask, and the answer is that "the Lord" needs it.
b: The owners are hoi kyrioi autou, literally "its lords," and the disciples answer "ho kyrios has need of it." Mark mentions only bystanders (Mark 11:5). Luke's wording sets the colt's legal owners before a higher Lord, whose claim they accept. In 19:31 and 19:34 "the Lord" may be Jesus, God, or even the colt's absent owner; Luke's readers would have heard it as Jesus.

a: set Jesus on it
p: Luke uses the verb of Solomon's coronation, when David's servants "set" Solomon on the king's mule.
b: When David made Solomon king, he ordered his officials to "set" Solomon on his own mule and lead him to Gihon to be anointed (1 Kings 1:33, 38, 44; the Septuagint uses epibibazō, the verb Luke uses here). When Jehu was proclaimed king, the officers spread their cloaks under him (2 Kings 9:13). So the disciples' actions in 19:35–36 are those of a coronation: the son of David is mounted and acclaimed as he approaches his city.

a: spreading their own cloaks
p: Luke has cloaks on the road but no branches or palms, and no "Hosanna."
b: Mark and Matthew have branches cut from the fields or trees; John has palm branches (John 12:13), the source of "Palm Sunday." Luke has only cloaks. Palm and leafy branches were associated with festivals and with the Maccabees' victory celebration (1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7), and Hosanna ("save now") had nationalist overtones. Many scholars think Luke, writing for Gentile readers in the Roman world, softened these signs of a Jewish national rising, while keeping the claim that Jesus is King.

a: the whole throng of disciples
p: In Luke the praise comes from Jesus' disciples, not from the city's crowds.
b: Mark speaks of "many" and Matthew of "the crowds" (Mark 11:8–9; Matthew 21:8–9). Luke specifies "the whole throng of disciples," the many followers who had come with him from Galilee, including the women (8:1–3; 23:49). They praise God for "all the acts of power they had seen," the healings and signs of the journey. This matters for how the Passion is read: the people who hailed Jesus as king are not the same as the crowd who later cried "Crucify" (23:21), a contrast often blurred in preaching.

a: Blessed is the King who comes in the Lord's name!
p: The disciples sing Psalm 118:26, the pilgrims' song, and add the word "King."
b: Psalm 118 was one of the Hallel psalms sung at the great festivals, and its line "Blessed is the one who comes in the LORD's name!" (Psalm 118:26) welcomed pilgrims to the temple. Of the first three Gospels, only Luke puts "the King" into the psalm verse, which makes the welcome a royal acclamation; John has "the King of Israel" (John 12:13), and Mark adds "our father David's kingdom" (Mark 11:10). Jesus had said that Jerusalem would not see him until they said these words (13:35). "The Lord" here translates the Greek kyrios, which stands for the divine name in the Hebrew.

a: In heaven, peace! And glory in the heights above!
p: At Jesus' birth the angels sang "peace on earth"; now his disciples sing "peace in heaven."
b: At the birth the heavenly army sang, "Glory to God in the heights above, and on earth peace" (2:14). Now the earthly disciples sing back, "In heaven, peace! And glory in the heights above!" The pairing is deliberate. Mark 11:10 and Matthew 21:9 have the same Greek phrase (en tois hypsistois), rendered "in the highest" on this site; Luke's Plain says "in the heights above" to keep the link with 2:14, where the Greek is the same. Some see a sad note: the peace meant for earth is now proclaimed only in heaven, because the city is about to reject it (19:42). Others read it as the earth's answer to heaven's song, peace now made between God and people.

a: the stones will shout it out
p: The saying recalls Habakkuk 2:11, where the stones of a house built by injustice cry out against it.
b: In Habakkuk 2:11 the stone in the wall cries out and the beam answers it, accusing the one who built his house by violence. Jesus may mean that creation itself would praise if people fell silent, or that the stones of Jerusalem would testify against the city that rejected its king. Just afterward Jesus says that not one stone will be left on another (19:44; 21:6). Luke alone has the Pharisees' objection and this reply.

a: he broke into tears over it
p: Only Luke tells of this. The verb means loud weeping, as at a funeral.
b: Klaiō is weeping aloud. Jesus weeps over the city as Jeremiah wept over Jerusalem before its fall (Jeremiah 9:1; 13:17) and as Elisha wept over the harm Hazael would do to Israel (2 Kings 8:11–12). He laments: the coming judgment is not something he desires. Luke has already given his lament "Jerusalem, Jerusalem" (13:34–35), and on the way to the cross he will tell the women of Jerusalem to weep for themselves and their children (23:28–31). Christians later used these texts against the Jewish people; Luke's tone is grief for his own city and people.

a: what leads to peace
p: Jerusalem's name was understood as "city of peace." The city did not recognize the things of its own peace.
b: The name Yerushalayim was explained in Jewish and Christian tradition as containing shalom, "peace" (compare Psalm 122:6, "Ask for peace for Jerusalem"; Hebrews 7:2 on Salem, "king of peace"). The things "that lead to peace" are the terms of peace, the way of making peace with an enemy (14:32 uses the same phrase of a king asking for terms). Jesus offered the peace announced at his birth (2:14) and at the entry (19:38). The sentence breaks off in Greek ("If only you had known...!"), a sign of grief.

a: a palisade of stakes
p: Titus' Roman army did exactly this: built earthworks, then a wall right around Jerusalem.
b: In AD 70 the Roman general Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian, besieged Jerusalem. Josephus, who was there, describes the siege ramps (whose timber the defenders burned) and then the wall of about seven kilometers that the soldiers built in three days around the whole city, so that no one could get in or out (Josephus, War 5.491–511). Starvation followed. The prophets had pictured Jerusalem's siege in the same terms (Isaiah 29:3; Ezekiel 4:2). Scholars debate whether Luke's wording shows that he wrote after AD 70; see the deep dive on chapter 21.

a: They will smash you flat, you and your children inside you
p: The verb edaphizō appears in the Septuagint of Psalm 137:9 and Hosea, where children are dashed down in war.
b: Luke's edaphiousin, "they will level to the ground," is a rare verb that the Greek Old Testament uses for the cruelty of a conquered city: "Happy is the one who grabs your babies and shatters them on the rock" (Psalm 137:9, where the Septuagint uses this verb), and in Hosea 10:14 and 13:16 and Nahum 3:10. Jerusalem's "children" are its people. The ancient world knew such slaughter: Josephus describes the killing in the city in AD 70 (War, book 6).

a: the season when you were visited
p: Episkopē is God's coming to his people, to save or to judge. Luke began his Gospel with it.
b: The Greek says only "the season of your visitation"; most readers take the visitor to be God, as in Luke's other uses of the word. Zechariah praised God because "he has visited his people and worked their redemption" (1:68; compare 1:78), and the crowd at Nain said, "God has visited his people!" (7:16). The same word, episkopē, was used in the Septuagint for God's coming to judge (Jeremiah 6:15; 10:15). Jerusalem's tragedy, as Luke tells it, is that the visit of salvation went unrecognized. The word also gives English "episcopal" (an overseer is one who visits and watches over).
orig: τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς σου (ton kairon tēs episkopēs sou)

a: began to throw out
p: Luke tells the temple action in two verses. There are no overturned tables, no money changers and no fig tree.
b: Mark gives the scene four verses and frames it with the cursing of the fig tree (Mark 11:12–25); John places it at the start of Jesus' ministry (John 2:13–22). Luke keeps only the expulsion and the saying, and moves at once to Jesus teaching in the temple every day (19:47). In Luke the temple is cleared so it can become what it was meant to be, a place of prayer and teaching. Luke's Gospel begins and ends in the temple (1:9; 24:53), and the first believers in Acts keep meeting there (Acts 2:46). On why Jesus acted, see the deep dives at Matthew 21 and Mark 11.

a: 'My house will be a house of prayer.'
p: Luke quotes Isaiah 56:7 but, like Matthew, stops before "for all the nations."
b: Isaiah promised that foreigners who keep the covenant would come to God's holy mountain, "for my house will be called a house of prayer for all the peoples" (Isaiah 56:7). Mark quotes the whole line (Mark 11:17). Luke, who cares most of all for the Gentiles, leaves it off. A common explanation: when Luke wrote, the temple was gone, and the nations were now being gathered elsewhere, through the apostles' preaching (24:47; Acts 1:8). The "cave for bandits" is from Jeremiah's temple sermon, which warned that the temple would be destroyed (Jeremiah 7:11–14).

a: the leading men of the people
p: The chief priests, the scribes and the people's leading men: the temple aristocracy, the legal experts and the lay nobility.
b: Luke names the groups who made up Jerusalem's ruling class and the Sanhedrin: the chief priests (the high priest and the senior priestly families), the scribes (experts in the Law), and "the first of the people," the wealthy lay elders. The Pharisees, Jesus' main critics on the journey, disappear from Luke's story after 19:39 and play no part in his death. Opposed to the leaders stands "the people" (ho laos), who listen eagerly (19:48; 21:38). Luke keeps this distinction until the trial, where the people are drawn in (23:13).

a: hung on him as they listened
p: Ekkremamai means to hang from something. The people were hanging on Jesus.
b: The verb appears only here in the New Testament. Greek writers used it of hanging on someone's lips or depending on someone completely. The people are the reason the leaders cannot act openly (20:19; 22:2), so they need a quiet arrest away from the crowd, which Judas will offer (22:3–6).

a: telling the good news
t: Teaching and telling the good news
p: Luke's favorite verb for preaching, euangelizomai, describes Jesus even in the temple courts.
b: Mark never uses the verb euangelizomai; Luke uses it ten times in the Gospel and fifteen in Acts. Jesus' mission began with Isaiah's words, "to bring good news to the poor" (4:18), and here, in the last week, he is still doing it in the temple. The question about his authority comes not from a scene of violence (Luke has just two verses on the temple action, 19:45–46) but from his daily teaching.

a: on what authority do you do these things?
p: The temple belonged to the priests. Who allowed this Galilean to drive out traders and teach in its courts?
b: The chief priests controlled the temple and its business; the scribes and elders sat with them on the council. A teacher who acted in the temple without their permission challenged their authority directly. Their question also sets a trap: if Jesus claims authority from God, it can be called blasphemy; if he claims none, he loses the people. On Jesus' counter-question about John, and on the scene in Mark and Matthew, see Mark 11:27–33.

a: The whole people will stone us
p: Only Luke says the leaders feared the people would stone them.
b: Mark and Matthew say the leaders feared the crowd. Luke makes it specific: the people would stone them, the punishment for a false prophet or a blasphemer (Deuteronomy 13:10; 17:5). If they denied that John was God's prophet, they would themselves be treated as speaking against God. Luke repeats that the people are on Jesus' side (19:48; 20:19, 26; 21:38). In Acts the temple guard avoids force with the apostles for the same reason: "they feared the people might stone them" (Acts 5:26).

a: A man planted a vineyard
p: Luke tells the parable without most of Mark's echoes of Isaiah 5: no hedge, no winepress, no tower.
b: In Isaiah 5:1–7 God plants a vineyard, Israel, and finds only bad grapes. Mark and Matthew describe the vineyard in Isaiah's words (hedge, winepress, tower). Luke keeps only "planted a vineyard," so the story is about the tenants rather than the vine. The Gospel of Thomas (saying 65), a sayings collection found in Egypt in 1945 that no church counts as Scripture, has a shorter form still. On the history and later use of the parable, see the notes and deep dive at Mark 12:1–12.

a: left the country for a long time
p: Large estates owned by absent landlords and worked by tenants were common in Galilee and Judea.
b: Papyri from Egypt and evidence from Judea show landowners leasing vineyards to tenant farmers for a share of the crop. A new vineyard took about four years to bear (Leviticus 19:23–25), so the owner's first claim would come years after planting. Luke alone adds "for a long time." Some readers see in it the long time of God's patience with Israel; others connect it with Luke's concern for the delay of the king's return (19:11–12).

a: Perhaps they will respect him
p: Only Luke has the owner wonder aloud, "What am I to do?" and "perhaps."
b: The owner's soliloquy is typical of Luke's parables: the rich fool (12:17), the dishonest manager (16:3) and the unjust judge (18:4) also talk to themselves. Isōs, "perhaps," is found nowhere else in the New Testament. The owner hopes; he does not know how the tenants will act. Readers have long noticed the pathos: the God of the parable does everything possible before judging.

a: my dearly loved son
p: These are the words the heavenly voice used of Jesus at the baptism.
b: "You are my dearly loved Son" (3:22) and "This is my Son, the Chosen One" (9:35). The parable's "dearly loved son" invites the hearer to see Jesus. The phrase echoes Genesis 22:2 (Isaac, "your son, your only son, whom you love"), and Mark 12:6 has the same words. Luke's tenants recognize who the son is and kill him because of it.

a: So they cast him outside the vineyard and killed him
p: Luke and Matthew put the throwing out before the killing; Mark has it after.
b: In Mark the farmers kill the son and then throw his body out (Mark 12:8). Matthew and Luke reverse the order: they throw him out, then kill him. Many see an adjustment to the passion story: Jesus was crucified outside the city (Hebrews 13:12–13; John 19:17, 20). That Matthew and Luke agree against Mark here is one of the "minor agreements" scholars weigh in the Synoptic problem.

a: That must never happen!
p: The people's horrified answer, mē genoito, is the phrase Paul uses fourteen times for "Absolutely not!"
b: Only Luke records a reply from the hearers. Mē genoito is a strong wish against something, "may it not happen," the phrase Paul uses in Romans when he rejects a false conclusion ("Has God rejected his people? Never!", Romans 11:1). The people of Jerusalem are horrified at the thought of the vineyard being given to others. The KJV's "God forbid" adds a word the Greek does not have, though it catches the tone.

a: 'A stone that the builders threw out has become the head of the corner'
p: Psalm 118:22, the same psalm the disciples just sang (19:38). Peter quotes it before the council (Acts 4:11).
b: Psalm 118 is the pilgrims' psalm: verse 26 was sung at the entry (19:38), and verse 22 now answers the leaders. The "head of the corner" is the main stone that holds two walls, or the capstone at the top. Luke quotes only verse 22, not verse 23. Peter quotes it to the same council ("the stone that you, the builders, treated as nothing," Acts 4:11), and 1 Peter 2:7 applies it to Christ. The quotation matches the site's Plain of Psalm 118:22 word for word.

a: it will scatter like chaff
p: This verse joins Isaiah's stone of stumbling with Daniel's stone that smashes the kingdoms.
b: "Anyone who falls on that stone will be shattered" recalls Isaiah 8:14–15, the stone over which many in Israel will stumble and be broken. "Anyone it falls on, it will scatter like chaff" recalls Daniel 2:34–35, 44–45, where a stone cut without hands smashes the statue of the world empires and the wind blows them away like chaff. The rare verb likmaō ("winnow, scatter like chaff") is used in the Greek of Daniel 2:44 (Theodotion's version). The Jewish midrash also joined such stone texts. The same verse in Matthew 21:44 is missing from some manuscripts and is thought to come from Luke.
r: Isaiah 8:14–15; Daniel 2:34–35; Daniel 2:44–45; Matthew 21:44; Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8

a: agents who acted as if they were righteous men
p: Enkathetoi are planted agents; hypokrinomai means to play a part on stage.
b: The verb hypokrinomai gives English "hypocrite": it is what an actor does. The spies pose as sincere, law-abiding Jews with an honest question. Luke leaves out who they are: Mark and Matthew name Pharisees and Herodians (Mark 12:13). Luke states their purpose openly: to hand Jesus over to "the governor," Pontius Pilate, whose name Luke has given in 3:1 and 13:1. The charge they will bring is exactly this: "He hinders people from paying taxes to Caesar" (23:2).

a: pay tribute to Caesar
p: Phoros was the tribute a conquered people paid Rome. Paying it meant accepting Roman rule.
b: Mark and Matthew use kēnsos, the Latin census, a head tax. Luke uses the ordinary Greek phoros, tribute paid by subject peoples (the same word Paul uses in Romans 13:6–7). Since Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6, its people paid tribute straight to Rome, and Judas the Galilean led a revolt saying that paying it meant accepting human masters in place of God (Josephus, Antiquities 18.4–10; Acts 5:37). A "yes" would anger nationalists; a "no" was treason.

a: Whose image and name does it have on it?
p: The silver denarius of Tiberius carried his portrait and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.
b: The common denarius of the emperor Tiberius (AD 14–37) showed his head with the Latin legend TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS, "Tiberius Caesar Augustus, son of the divine Augustus," and on the back a seated woman often identified as his mother Livia, with the words PONTIF MAXIM (high priest). To many Jews such a coin, with a human image and a claim of divinity, was offensive in the holy city. Jesus does not carry one; his questioners produce it. On the saying itself and its long history in the churches, see the card on Matthew 22.

a: pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God
t: Was Jesus accused of the opposite?
p: Luke tells the answer plainly, then reports that Jesus was later accused of forbidding the tax (23:2).
b: Luke writes as if to answer a Roman reader's worry: was Jesus a rebel against Rome? Here he says to pay what is owed, yet at the trial the leaders accuse him: "He hinders people from paying taxes to Caesar" (23:2), a charge Luke's reader knows to be false. Pilate declares him innocent three times (23:4, 14, 22). Luke-Acts shows Roman officials again and again finding the Christians harmless (Acts 18:14–15; 23:29; 26:31–32). How far the saying limits Caesar's claim (since a human being bears God's image) is debated; see Matthew 22.

a: the ones who deny there is any resurrection
p: This is the only time the Sadducees appear in Luke's Gospel. Acts will explain them further.
b: The Sadducees were the party of the high priestly families and the wealthy aristocracy. Josephus says they held that souls perish with the body and accepted only the written law, not the Pharisees' traditions (Antiquities 18.16; 13.297). Acts adds that they "claim there is no resurrection, no angel, and no spirit" (Acts 23:8). They will lead the opposition to the apostles in Acts 4:1–2 and 5:17, "deeply upset that these two were teaching the people and declaring that in Jesus there is resurrection from the dead" (Acts 4:2).

a: raise up descendants for his brother
p: The Sadducees cite Deuteronomy 25:5–6, the duty of a brother-in-law to marry a dead brother's widow.
b: Under the law of levirate marriage (from Latin levir, "husband's brother"), when a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow, and the first son would carry the dead man's name (Deuteronomy 25:5–6; Genesis 38:8; Ruth 4:5, 10). The Sadducees' story is a joke meant to make the resurrection absurd. On the custom and its later history, see Mark 12:19 and the levirate marriage topic.

a: The children of this age
p: "Sons of" is a Hebrew way of saying "people who belong to." Luke alone sets "this age" against "that age."
b: "Children of this age" (literally "sons") are people who belong to the present world, as in 16:8 ("the children of this age are shrewder than the children of light"). Mark and Matthew have only the statement that the risen do not marry. Luke builds a contrast between two ages (18:30): in this age people marry, because they die and need children; in the age to come, people who no longer die do not. In this age, men took wives and fathers gave daughters in marriage; the Greek has the two verbs for the man's part and the woman's part.

a: found worthy to reach that age
p: Luke speaks only of those "found worthy" of the resurrection. Does he mean all people will not rise?
b: Luke's wording, "those found worthy to reach that age and the resurrection from the dead," describes the resurrection to life. Some readers take it to mean that only the righteous rise, as some Jewish texts teach (Psalms of Solomon 3:12). But Paul in Acts speaks of a resurrection "of the righteous and the unrighteous alike" (Acts 24:15; compare Luke 14:14, "the resurrection of the righteous"; Daniel 12:2; John 5:28–29). Most readers hold that Jesus is speaking here of the life of the saved, without denying the judgment of all. The question is set out on the card at Acts 24:15.

a: They are the equals of angels
p: Jewish writings also said the righteous will be like angels. The Sadducees did not believe in angels at all.
b: Isangeloi, "angel-equal," appears only here. Jewish texts of the time say the righteous will shine like stars and become like angels (Daniel 12:3; 1 Enoch 104:4–6; 2 Baruch 51:10). 1 Enoch 15:6–7 explains that the spirits of heaven do not marry because they do not die. A later rabbinic saying puts it this way: "In the world to come there is no eating or drinking, no having children," but the righteous sit and enjoy the radiance of God's presence (Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 17a). Jesus does not say the risen are angels or lose their bodies (24:39), only that they no longer marry or die.
r: Daniel 12:2–3; 24:39; 1 Enoch 15:6–7; 1 Enoch 104:4–6; 2 Baruch 51:10; Acts 23:8; 1 Corinthians 15:42–44

a: children of God, being children of the resurrection
p: The risen are God's children because the resurrection is a new birth from God.
b: Being raised makes them "sons of God," a Hebrew idiom for people who share God's life (compare 6:35, "you will be sons of the Most High"). Paul calls the resurrection the "adoption, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23) and calls Jesus "declared Son of God in power by the resurrection from the dead" (Romans 1:4). Eastern Christian writers took the verse into their teaching on theosis, sharing in God's life.

a: even Moses made known, in the passage about the bush
p: The Sadducees accepted the books of Moses as authority, so Jesus answers from Exodus 3, not from the Prophets.
b: Daniel 12:2 states the resurrection plainly, but the Sadducees gave final authority to the five books of Moses. So Jesus argues from Exodus 3:6, the burning bush: "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob." Before chapter and verse numbers, passages were cited by a key word: "at the bush." The rabbis also argued the resurrection from the Torah (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 90b–91b). Luke says Moses "calls the Lord" this, perhaps following Exodus 3:15, where God gives this name "for all time."

a: for to him all are alive
p: Only Luke adds this line, which matches a saying in 4 Maccabees about the martyrs.
b: 4 Maccabees, a Jewish book from about the first century AD, says that those who die for God do not die to God, as the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did not, but live to God (4 Maccabees 7:19; compare 4 Maccabees 16:25). 4 Maccabees is in the Greek Orthodox Bible as an appendix and is not counted as Scripture by Catholics or Protestants. Luke's line may mean that the dead are alive to God now, in some form, and will rise; or that God sees them as alive because he will certainly raise them. The verse is used on both sides of the debate over the state of the dead; see the card at 16:19–31.

a: That was well said, Teacher.
p: Some scribes, probably Pharisees, approve Jesus' answer. Luke has moved the question of the greatest commandment elsewhere.
b: The Pharisees and their scribes believed in the resurrection (Acts 23:6–9), so they welcome a defeat of the Sadducees. In Mark the friendly scribe then asks which commandment is first (Mark 12:28–34). Luke has already told a version of that exchange, with a lawyer, before the good Samaritan (10:25–28), so here he keeps only the scribes' approval and the silence that follows (20:40). In Acts the Pharisee Gamaliel and others will likewise side with the apostles against the Sadducees (Acts 5:34–39; 23:9).

a: In what way do people say the Messiah is David's son?
p: Jesus does not deny that the Messiah is David's son; Luke has said Jesus is (1:32; 18:38). He asks how he can be more.
b: Luke's angel told Mary that her son would have "the throne of David his father" (1:32), and Luke traces Jesus' family through David (3:31). So the question is not a denial, but a riddle: if David calls the Messiah "my Lord" in Psalm 110, the Messiah must be greater than David's son in the ordinary sense. Luke answers it in Acts 2:34–36, where Peter quotes the same psalm and concludes that God has made the crucified Jesus "both Lord and Messiah."

a: 'The Lord said to my Lord
p: The Old Testament verse quoted most often in the New. In Hebrew it reads "The LORD declares to my lord."
b: In Hebrew the first "Lord" is the divine name YHWH and the second is adoni, "my lord": "The LORD declares to my lord: 'Sit at my right hand'" (Psalm 110:1). The Greek, which Luke follows, has kyrios for both, which makes the riddle sharper. Luke alone says "in the book of Psalms," as he does in Acts 1:20. Luke's wording of 20:42–43 matches Peter's quotation in Acts 2:34–35 exactly, and this site gives them the same Plain. The psalm is quoted or echoed in Hebrews 1:13; 1 Corinthians 15:25; and Jesus' answer at his trial (22:69).

a: Watch out for the scribes
t: A warning to disciples, heard by all
p: Luke has Jesus speak to his disciples while the people listen. The warning targets a type, not every scribe.
b: Luke's version is close to Mark 12:38–40, not to Matthew's long chapter of woes (Matthew 23). Luke has already given woes against Pharisees and lawyers at a dinner (11:37–52). Here the hearers are the disciples, who will be the church's leaders; the same temptations of status apply to them (22:24–27). Just before, "some of the scribes" agreed with Jesus (20:39), so Luke's readers should not hear this as a judgment on every scribe or on Judaism as such.

a: They eat up widows' houses
p: How did scribes devour widows' houses? Perhaps as trustees of their property, taking fees or worse.
b: Several explanations have been offered: scribes acting as legal guardians or trustees of widows' estates took large fees or mismanaged them; they accepted lavish hospitality from widows who could not afford it; or they encouraged widows to give their means to the temple. Luke's next scene, a widow giving everything to the temple (21:1–4), makes the last possibility pointed. See Mark 12:40 for the same saying.

a: the treasury
p: The treasury was a set of trumpet-shaped offering chests in the Court of the Women.
b: The Mishnah describes thirteen offering chests shaped like trumpets in the temple, each marked for a different purpose (Mishnah Shekalim 6:5). They stood in the Court of the Women, where men and women could go. John 8:20 also mentions Jesus teaching "in the treasury." Luke's scene follows Mark 12:41–44 closely but is shorter.

a: two lepta
p: The lepton was the smallest copper coin in use, a tiny fraction of a day's wage.
b: A lepton ("small one") was a small bronze coin minted by the Hasmonean kings and the Roman governors in Judea. Mark explains to his readers that two lepta made a Roman quadrans (Mark 12:42), one sixty-fourth of a denarius; Luke leaves the explanation out. The KJV's "two mites" gave English the phrase "the widow's mite." Luke calls her penichra, "needy," and then ptōchē, "poor" (21:3), the word of "Blessed are you poor" (6:20).

a: she, out of her lack, dropped in her whole living
p: Is the widow a model of generosity, or a victim of a system that took her last coins?
b: The traditional reading takes her as the model giver: she gave not out of surplus but everything. Addison Wright argued that, coming right after the warning against those who "eat up widows' houses" (20:47) and right before the prophecy that the temple will be destroyed (21:6), the scene is a lament: Jesus grieves that religious teaching has led a poor widow to give her whole living to a doomed institution. Many scholars now hold both: Jesus honors her devotion, and the context condemns those who profit from it. "Her whole living" (bios) means all she had to live on.

a: decked out with fine stones and dedicated gifts
p: Herod's rebuilding of the temple was among the wonders of the age. Gifts from kings hung on its walls.
b: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple about 20 BC, and work went on until the 60s AD (compare John 2:20). Josephus describes white stones of enormous size, some over forty feet long, a front covered with gold that blinded the eye in sunlight, and a golden vine over the sanctuary door with grape clusters as tall as a man (War 5.184–227; Antiquities 15.391–402). The "dedicated gifts" (anathēmata) were offerings hung in the temple; Josephus mentions gifts from foreign rulers. The rabbis said, "Whoever has not seen Herod's building has never seen a beautiful building" (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 4a). In Luke "some people" speak, not a disciple as in Mark, and the scene stays in the temple.

a: not one stone will be left on a stone
p: The Romans burned the temple in August AD 70 and later leveled what was left.
b: Titus' army took the temple area in the summer of AD 70; the sanctuary burned, and Josephus says the city was afterward torn down except for three towers and part of the western wall, to show how strong the place had been (War 6.249–266; 7.1–4). The great stones of the retaining wall can still be seen where Roman soldiers pushed them down onto the street below. The Western Wall is part of the platform's retaining wall, not the temple itself. On the discourse that follows and how it is read, see the deep dives on Matthew 24 and Mark 13.

a: when, then, will this happen?
p: In Luke the disciples ask only about the temple's destruction, not about "your coming and the end of the age."
b: In Matthew the disciples ask about the temple and about Jesus' coming and the end of the age (Matthew 24:3); in Mark, about "all these things" (Mark 13:4). Luke's question concerns only when the temple will fall and what sign will warn of it. Luke's answer keeps the two subjects more clearly apart than Mark or Matthew: the fall of Jerusalem (21:20–24) and, after the "times of the Gentiles," the coming of the Son of Man (21:25–28). In Luke the scene is still in the temple courts; the Mount of Olives is mentioned only in 21:37.

a: 'The time has drawn near.'
t: The false message: the end is now
p: Only Luke warns against those who say "the time is near." Luke treats an immediate end as a false teaching.
b: Jesus himself and John the Baptist announced that the kingdom "has drawn near" (10:9, 11). Yet here, people who say "The time has drawn near" are false guides. Hans Conzelmann argued that Luke wrote to calm a church disappointed that Jesus had not yet returned: the end is certain but not immediate (19:11; Acts 1:6–7). Others note that Luke still expects the end (21:32, 36) and warns only against those who set dates. "I am he" (egō eimi) may be a claim to be the Messiah, or to be Jesus come back, or an echo of God's own name.

a: the end will not come right away
p: Mark says "the end is not yet"; Luke says "not immediately" and adds "first."
b: Luke adds two small words that push the end further away: "These things have to happen first," and the end will come "not right away" (ouk eutheōs). "Uprisings" (akatastasiai, disorders, revolts) fits the civil wars that tore the Roman world after Nero's death in AD 68, the "year of the four emperors," and the Jewish revolt itself.

a: famines and plagues
p: Luke adds plagues to famines, a sound play in Greek: limoi and loimoi.
b: Greek writers often paired limos (famine) and loimos (plague), since one followed the other; Hesiod already joined them. Luke alone has "plagues" here, and "terrors, and great signs from the sky." Josephus lists omens before Jerusalem's fall: a star like a sword over the city, a comet for a year, a light around the altar at night, the great eastern gate opening by itself, and chariots and armed men seen in the clouds (War 6.288–300). The Talmud also records signs in the temple during its last forty years (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 39b). Luke's famine under Claudius is in Acts 11:28.

a: drag you off before kings and governors
p: Luke's readers would see this verse played out in Acts, step by step.
b: Peter and John are arrested and put in prison (Acts 4:3; 5:18); James is killed and Peter jailed by King Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12:1–4); Paul is beaten in synagogues, imprisoned, and brought before the governors Felix and Festus and King Agrippa II (Acts 22:19; 24–26). Luke changes Mark's "councils" to "prisons" and says "Ahead of all these things": the persecution of the church comes before the fall of Jerusalem. "Because of my name" is a phrase Acts repeats (Acts 5:41; 9:16).
r: Acts 4:3; Acts 5:18; Acts 12:1–4; Acts 22:19; Acts 24:1–27; Acts 25:23; Acts 5:41; Mark 13:9

a: I myself will give you a mouth and wisdom
p: In Mark the Holy Spirit speaks through them; here Jesus himself gives the words, as God promised Moses.
b: God told Moses, who said he could not speak well, "I myself will be with your mouth and will teach you what to say" (Exodus 4:12). In Luke 12:12 the Holy Spirit teaches the disciples what to say; here Jesus promises that he himself will give "a mouth and wisdom." Acts shows it happening: Stephen's opponents "were no match for the wisdom and the Spirit he spoke with" (Acts 6:10), where the Greek uses the same verb antistēnai, and the council marveled at the boldness of uneducated Peter and John (Acts 4:13–14).

a: handed over even by parents, brothers, relatives and friends
p: Micah 7:6 had described a time when a person's enemies are in his own house.
b: "A man's enemies are the people of his own house" (Micah 7:6). Jesus earlier said he came to bring division even within families (12:51–53, quoting Micah). In the Roman world, Christians could be denounced to the authorities by relatives; Tacitus says that under Nero many were convicted on information given by others (Annals 15.44), and Pliny's letter to Trajan (about AD 112) mentions anonymous accusations.

a: not one hair from your head will be lost
t: Killed, yet not a hair lost?
p: Right after "some of you will be executed," Jesus says not a hair will perish. How can both be true?
b: The promise cannot mean that no disciple will die, since 21:16 says some will. Most readers take it of final safety: whatever happens to the body, nothing of the person is lost to God, who will raise them (12:4–7, "even the hairs on your head have all been counted"). Others take it as a general promise of God's care through suffering, a proverb drawn from 1 Samuel 14:45 and 2 Samuel 14:11. Paul uses the same proverb in a shipwreck (Acts 27:34).

a: by holding out
