p: Psychē means life, self or soul. The command is to keep one's true life by enduring.
b: Ktēsasthe tas psychas hymōn, "acquire your lives/souls." The KJV's "In your patience possess ye your souls" has become a proverb about keeping calm. The Greek hypomonē is not patience in the sense of calm waiting, but holding out under pressure, endurance. Mark has "whoever holds out to the end, that person will be saved" (Mark 13:13). Luke speaks of "lives" because the body may be killed (21:16), yet the self is kept, as in 9:24: "anyone who loses his life because of me, that person will save it." Some manuscripts have the future tense, a promise rather than a command (see the variant).
orig: ἐν τῇ ὑπομονῇ ὑμῶν (en tē hypomonē hymōn)

a: When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps
p: Where Mark has "the abomination of desolation," Luke has armies around Jerusalem. Does this show Luke wrote after AD 70?
b: Mark 13:14 speaks in Daniel's riddle: "When you see 'the abomination of desolation' standing where he must not stand." Luke gives a plain historical picture: Jerusalem surrounded by armies, its "desolation" near. Many scholars hold that Luke rewrote Mark in the light of what happened in AD 70, and use this verse to date Luke after that year. Others answer that a siege is the most obvious way to picture a city's fall, that the prophets described Jerusalem's sieges in these terms (Isaiah 29:3; Jeremiah 6:6; Ezekiel 4:1–3), and that Luke says nothing of the temple's burning or of the city's famine; C. H. Dodd and Bo Reicke argued that the language comes from the Old Testament and from the fall of 587 BC, not from AD 70. The deep dive on this chapter weighs the arguments; on Daniel's phrase, see Mark 13:14 and Matthew 24:15.
r: Mark 13:14; Matthew 24:15; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 12:11; 19:43; Isaiah 29:3; Ezekiel 4:1–3

a: Those inside the city must get out
p: Church historians later said the Jerusalem Christians fled across the Jordan to Pella before the siege.
b: Eusebius, writing about AD 325, reports that the church in Jerusalem, warned by a revelation, left the city before the war and settled in Pella, a town of the Decapolis east of the Jordan (Church History 3.5.3). Epiphanius tells the same story in the late 300s. Some historians doubt it, since the reports are late and the region was itself at war in AD 66–67; others accept a real core. Luke's advice is the opposite of what people usually did in war: they fled into walled cities. Here the walled city is the place of danger.

a: days of retribution
p: Hosea called a coming judgment "the days of punishment." Luke adds that all that is written will be fulfilled.
b: The phrase echoes Hosea 9:7 (in Greek, "the days of retribution have come") and Deuteronomy 32:35. "Retribution" (ekdikēsis) is the same word as the "justice" the widow demanded and God promised (18:3, 7–8): God's justice can mean rescue for some and judgment for others. Luke adds that these days fulfill "all that is written," pointing to the prophets' warnings of Jerusalem's fall, among them Jeremiah 7:14, Micah 3:12 and Daniel 9:26.
r: Hosea 9:7; Deuteronomy 32:35; Jeremiah 46:10; 18:7–8; Daniel 9:26; Micah 3:12; Jeremiah 7:14

a: wrath on this people
t: "This people" and the long misuse of this verse
p: Jesus speaks as a Jewish prophet grieving over his own people. Christians later read the verse as God's permanent rejection of the Jews.
b: "Wrath on this people" stands in the line of the prophets, who announced God's judgment on Jerusalem from within Israel and wept over it (Jeremiah, Lamentations). From the second century, many Christian writers read Jerusalem's fall as God's final verdict on the Jewish people for rejecting Jesus, and this reading fed centuries of contempt. Luke's own story does not support a final rejection: Jesus weeps over the city (19:41), prays for those who crucify him (23:34, in most manuscripts; see the variant there), and in Acts thousands of Jews in Jerusalem believe (Acts 2:41; 21:20). The judgment is limited "until" (21:24). See the anti-Judaism topic and the deep dive on this chapter.

a: They will be cut down by the sword and carried off as prisoners into all the nations
p: Josephus gives the toll of the war: over a million dead, he says, and 97,000 taken captive.
b: Josephus says that 1,100,000 died in the siege and 97,000 were taken prisoner, many sent to the mines of Egypt or to die in arenas in the provinces (War 6.418–420). Modern historians think his total for the dead is greatly inflated, but the disaster was immense. The Arch of Titus in Rome, still standing, shows soldiers carrying the temple's lampstand in triumph. The Greek "by the mouth of the sword" (Plain: "cut down by the sword") and "captive into all the nations" echo Deuteronomy 28:64 and Jeremiah 21:7.

a: Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled
p: Only Luke has this phrase. The "until" suggests a limit to Jerusalem's fall. Readers disagree about what comes after.
b: "Trampled" echoes Zechariah 12:3 in Greek ("a stone trampled by all the nations"), Daniel 8:13 and Isaiah 63:18, and Revelation 11:2 (the nations "will trample the holy city for forty-two months"). The "times of the Gentiles" have been read as: the period of Gentile rule over Jerusalem, which some ended in 1967 when Israel took the Old City; the period of the Gentile mission (Romans 11:25, "until the full number of the Gentiles has come in"), after which Israel will turn to its Messiah; or simply the age between AD 70 and Christ's return, with no special future for Jerusalem. The card below sets out the church positions.
r: Zechariah 12:3; Daniel 8:13; Isaiah 63:18; Revelation 11:2; Romans 11:25–26; Acts 1:6–7; Tobit 14:5

a: the roar of the sea and the heaving waves
p: Prophets used the shaking of sun, moon, stars and sea as pictures of God's judgment on nations.
b: Isaiah 13:10 (the fall of Babylon) and Ezekiel 32:7 (the fall of Pharaoh) describe the sun and moon darkened. The roaring sea is the ancient picture of chaos and of raging nations (Psalm 65:7; Isaiah 17:12; Psalm 46:3). Readers differ: some take these signs literally, as events in nature before Christ's return; others as the prophets' picture language for the fall of world powers; others as both. Luke does not quote Isaiah's words as Mark does (Mark 13:24–25), but paraphrases and adds the sea.
r: Isaiah 13:10; Ezekiel 32:7–8; Joel 2:30–31; Psalm 65:7; Isaiah 17:12–13; Revelation 6:12–14; Acts 2:19–20

a: the powers in the heavens will be shaken
p: The phrase comes from Isaiah 34:4 in Greek, where the powers of heaven dissolve.
b: Mark 13:25 quotes from the Greek of Isaiah 34:4 ("all the powers of the heavens will melt"; the Hebrew has "the whole army of heaven will rot"). "Powers" can mean the heavenly bodies, which the ancients often thought of as ruling forces, or spiritual powers. Haggai 2:6, quoted in Hebrews 12:26–27, promises that God will "shake the heavens and the earth" once more, so that what cannot be shaken will remain. "The inhabited world" (oikoumenē) is Luke's word for the whole Roman world (2:1; Acts 17:6, 31).
r: Isaiah 34:4; Haggai 2:6; Hebrews 12:26–27; Mark 13:25; 2:1; Acts 17:6; Acts 17:31

a: coming in a cloud
p: Luke has "a cloud," singular, where Mark has "clouds." In Acts, Jesus leaves in a cloud and will return the same way.
b: Daniel 7:13 sees "one like a son of man" coming "with the clouds of heaven" to the Ancient of Days. Mark and Matthew have "clouds." Luke's singular cloud links this verse to the transfiguration cloud (9:34–35) and to the ascension: "a cloud received him" (Acts 1:9), and "this same Jesus ... will come this same way, just as you watched him go into the sky" (Acts 1:11). Luke thus reads the coming of the Son of Man as Jesus' personal return. Some preterist readers take the coming in Daniel's sense, an arrival before God to receive authority, which they see fulfilled in the resurrection and in AD 70; see the card on Matthew 24.

a: your redemption is getting close
p: Apolytrōsis is release by payment, the freeing of a slave or a prisoner. Luke uses it only here.
b: The word belongs to the family of "ransom" (lytron, Mark 10:45). Anna spoke to "everyone who was looking for Jerusalem to be redeemed" (2:38), and the disciples at Emmaus had hoped Jesus was "the man who would redeem Israel" (24:21). Here the redemption is final release at the coming of the Son of Man. Paul uses the same word for "the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23). While others faint with fear (21:26), disciples are told to stand up straight, as people about to be set free.

a: See the fig tree, and every tree
p: Luke adds "and every tree," perhaps for readers outside Palestine who did not know fig trees.
b: Mark and Matthew speak only of the fig tree, whose late leaves in spring signal summer (Mark 13:28). Luke widens it to all trees, a sign any reader could see. He also does not tell the cursing of the fig tree (Mark 11:12–14, 20–21), but he has told the parable of the barren fig tree given one more year (13:6–9).

a: know that the kingdom of God is near
p: Where Mark has "it is near" or "he is near," Luke spells out: the kingdom of God.
b: Mark's "know that it is near" (Mark 13:29) is ambiguous: he, or it? Luke makes the subject the kingdom of God, in its full arrival. Yet in Luke the kingdom is also already present in Jesus (11:20; 17:21). Luke holds both: the kingdom has come near in Jesus' ministry and will come in fullness when the Son of Man returns.

a: this generation will not be gone before it all happens
p: Luke keeps Mark's saying, but changes "all these things" to "it all." What did he think it meant?
b: The saying is one of the hardest in the Gospels; its readings (Jesus' own contemporaries and AD 70; the generation that sees the signs; "this kind" of people; a mistaken expectation) are set out in the notes on Mark 13:30 and Matthew 24:34 and on the card at Matthew 24:29–34. In Luke, who wrote a generation or more after Jesus, "generation" may mean the human race or the unbelieving "generation" Jesus rebuked (9:41; 11:29–32; 17:25), since Luke already places a long "times of the Gentiles" between Jerusalem's fall and the end (21:24). Others think Luke meant that the events beginning in AD 70 were the start of "it all."

a: my words will never be gone
p: Jesus claims for his words what Isaiah said of God's word.
b: "The grass dries up, the flower wilts, but our God's word will stand forever" (Isaiah 40:8). Earlier in Luke, Jesus said it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of the Law to drop out (16:17). Here his own words are what outlast the universe.

a: wild partying and drinking and the worries of making a living
p: Kraipalē is the headache after a drinking bout. Luke sets it beside ordinary worries as equally dangerous.
b: Kraipalē means the hangover after heavy drinking, or the carousing that causes it. The "worries of making a living" (merimnai biōtikai) are the same worries that choke the seed in the parable of the sower (8:14). Luke's warning reaches both the careless and the anxious: both make the heart "heavy," dull and sleepy, unready for the day. Paul gives a similar warning about the day coming like a thief, with drunkenness and sleep (1 Thessalonians 5:2–8).

a: like a snare
p: Isaiah 24:17 warned of "terror, trench and trap" for all who live on the earth.
b: "Terror, trench and trap are over you, you who live on the earth!" (Isaiah 24:17). A pagis is a bird trap that springs shut without warning. The day will not affect only Judea, as the siege did (21:21), but "everyone settled on the face of all the earth." On where to divide 21:34 and 21:35, see the variant.

a: to take your stand before the Son of Man
t: Standing before the Son of Man
p: To stand before a judge means to be acquitted. The disciples should pray to be found standing on that day.
b: In Jewish language, to "stand" before God or the king at the judgment means to pass the judgment and be accepted (Psalm 1:5, "the wicked will not stand when judgment comes"; Malachi 3:2, "Who can stand when he appears?"; Revelation 6:17). Luke's discourse ends with prayer, as this last stretch of teaching began with a parable on prayer (18:1): "stay alert ... keep praying." Some dispensational readers take "escape all these things" as a promise that the church will be taken away before the great suffering; most others read it as being kept safe through it, or passing the judgment. See the card on Matthew 24:40.

a: camped on the Mount of Olives
t: Nights on the Mount of Olives
p: Jesus did not stay in the city at night. Pilgrims filled Jerusalem at Passover, and many camped outside.
b: The verb aulizomai means to spend the night, often in the open. At Passover, pilgrims from all over the world crowded into Jerusalem, and many camped on the hills around it. Luke says Jesus went to the Mount of Olives "as he usually did" (22:39), which is how Judas knew where to find him. Mark says he stayed at Bethany (Mark 11:11), on the far side of the same hill.

a: all the people would get up at dawn
t: Where some manuscripts put the woman caught in adultery
p: A group of medieval manuscripts places the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53–8:11) right after this verse.
b: The story of the woman caught in adultery is not found in the oldest manuscripts of John. It "floats" in the later manuscripts: most place it after John 7:52, some after John 7:36 or 21:25, and the manuscripts of family 13 (a group of related Greek copies from the 1000s on) place it here, after Luke 21:38. The setting fits: Jesus teaching in the temple at dawn, "all the people" coming to him (compare John 8:2). Its style is also closer to Luke's in some ways. Luke's own text does not include it. See the deep dive on John 7:53–8:11.
